## Slide 2 · Goals for today

Three goals today. You learn how to set up an R project, you learn about the
difference between absolute and relative paths, and you learn how to use the
`here` package.

This session looks like the least exciting of the semester and is in fact one of
the most consequential: almost every "it works on my machine" problem you will
have later traces back to what we discuss today.

## Slide 4 · Our goal

The goal of this session is that you learn about a default directory structure
and a general way to document everything you do in your project. This
facilitates the collaboration with future-you considerably — and nothing is
worse than hating your past-you for not documenting correctly where data came
from, or how it has been prepared.

We also want a general workflow to avoid problems in the context of project
management.

The central idea behind all of it: all results must be reproducible from the raw
data. That has one immediate consequence — you must not manipulate your raw
data. Raw data is what you download from the internet, gather through an
experiment, or code yourself, and it stays exactly as it arrived.

## Slide 5 · How to keep your work transparent

Raw data must not be changed, but it is usually not in a state we can work with.
The way out is a four-step loop.

First, gather the data and save it on your computer. Second, import this data
into R. Third, write a script that transforms the raw data into tidy data.
Fourth, use the tidy data for the actual analysis: visualisation, modelling and
so on.

Saving the scripts in steps two and three makes your work fully reproducible.
The scripts always tell you what you did to your raw data — which means you can
heal basically every mistake you made. If you had instead edited the raw file in
Excel, the mistake would be permanent and invisible.

## Slide 6 · Where we are heading

Here is the map for the next few sessions. Setting up your project environment
is done only once per project. Importing data, transforming raw data into tidy
data and saving data may be done several times, in a loop.

Today we deal with the first box only. It is the box that everybody is tempted
to skip, and the one that decides whether the following weeks are pleasant or
painful.

## Slide 8 · Setting up your working environment

Where you save your data and your files is important — much more important than
it looks at first.

The right directory structure is a prerequisite for a transparent, reproducible
and easy-to-work-with project. For every task in R you should set up your
project like the tree on the right: a project folder containing the `.Rproj`
file, a `data` folder split into `raw` and `tidy`, an `R` folder for the
scripts, an `output` folder for results, and `misc` for everything else.

The split between `data/raw` and `data/tidy` is the structural expression of the
rule from the previous slide: raw data goes into `raw` and is never touched
again; everything your scripts produce goes into `tidy`.

All relevant steps to set this up, and the rationale for this structure, are
described in the respective tutorial.

## Slide 9 · Creating an R project

The concrete click-by-click steps for creating an R project are documented in
the associated tutorial and video, so we do not spend session time on them. The
slides focus on selected background concepts only — the things that are worth
discussing together because they are conceptually tricky rather than mechanical.

## Slide 11 · Absolute and relative paths

There are two ways to tell your computer where a certain file is located.

Via an absolute path, where the description starts at the root directory of your
file system — the very top. Or via a relative path, where the description starts
at your current position in the file system, the working directory.

The screenshot shows the situation: we are located in the folder
DataScienceExercises, framed in red, and we want to point to the file
`nycflights21_small.rda` inside its `data` folder.

## Slide 12 · The same file, two descriptions

Here are the two descriptions of one and the same file. The absolute path starts
at Volumes and spells out every level. The relative path is simply
`data/nycflights21_small.rda`.

The relative path seems nicer for two reasons. It is shorter. And, much more
importantly, you can share your code without forcing others to adjust the path —
because on their machine the project sits somewhere else entirely, but the
`data` folder is still inside it.

## Slide 13 · Relative paths and `setwd()`

So the relative path is nicer — but it raises a problem: how do we set our
location to the directory DataScienceExercises in the first place?

One option is to use `setwd()` and provide the absolute path to
DataScienceExercises as an argument. Then we can use the short relative path
afterwards. And indeed, many people put `setwd()` at the top of their scripts.

You must never ever do this. The next slide explains why.

## Slide 14 · Why `setwd()` is evil

Why is `setwd()` evil?

First, it does not even solve the problem it appears to solve. You wanted to
avoid absolute paths — and to use `setwd()` you have to write an absolute path.
The absolute path has not disappeared, it has only moved to line one.

Second, it makes others hate you. Abby writes a script with `setwd()` at the top
and sends it to Ellie. Ellie opens the file and executes it, and gets an error:
cannot change working directory. The folder in Abby's path exists on Abby's
machine and nowhere else in the universe.

And note that "others" includes future-you on a new laptop.

## Slide 15 · The better alternative: `here`

The simple solution is the package `here`.

It sets an anchor in your project directory. You then create all paths relative
to this anchor using `here::here()` — and because the anchor is found by looking
for the project file rather than by hard-coding a location, this will always work
on every machine.

The way to set the anchor is to put `here::i_am()` into the very first line of
your script, telling it where this script sits inside the project. From then on,
`here::here("data", "raw", "file.csv")` gives you a correct absolute path on any
computer, without you ever writing one.

So: `here::i_am()` in line one, always. It costs you one line and saves you the
entire class of problems from the previous slide.

## Slide 16 · Your turn

Your turn. Create a new R project on your computer and create all the required
folders from the tree. Then write an R script, put it into the right directory —
that is, into `R` — and make it usable for the `here` package by adding the
`i_am()` line.

Then check out what the function `here::here()` actually returns when you call
it with and without arguments, and experiment with its use. Seeing the absolute
path it builds for you is what makes the concept click.

## Slide 17 · Summary and outlook

To summarise: we now know how to organise our working directory. We know the
important difference between absolute and relative paths. And we know that the
challenge of using code on different machines can be addressed with the `here`
package, which is the better alternative to `setwd()`.

Project management is essential but often under-appreciated — it is invisible
when it works and catastrophic when it does not.

Two further topics point beyond this session: using a version control system
such as Git, and using virtual programming environments, for example via the
package `renv`. Both are covered in the tutorials for those who want to go
further.
